source_text: Quid autem ad caetera respondebimus? Primo enim, si ex mortuis vivi, sicut mortui ex vivis, unus omnino et idem numerus semper haesisset omnium, ille scilicet numerus qui primus vitam introisset, priores enim mortuis vivi, dehinc mortui ex vivis, et rursus ex mortuis vivi. Et dum hoc semper ex iisdem, ita totidem semper qui ex iisdem; neque plures aut pauciores exissent, quam redirent. Invenimus autem apud commentarios etiam humanarum antiquitatum, paulatim humanum genus exuberasse, dum aborigines, vel vagi, vel extorres, vel gloriosi quique occupant terras, ut Scythae Parthicas, ut Amyclae Peloponesum, ut Athenienses Asiam, ut Phryges Italiam, ut Phoenices Africam, dum solennes etiam migrationes, quas ἀποικίας appellant, consilio exonerandae popularitatis, in alios fines examina gentis eructant. Nam et aborigines nunc in suis sedibus permanent, et alibi amplius gentilitatem foeneraverunt. Certe quidem ipse orbis in promptu est, cultior de die, et instructior pristino. Omnia jam pervia, omnia nota, omnia negotiosa; solitudines famosas retro fundi amoenissimi obliteraverunt; sylvas arva domuerunt; feras pecora fugaverunt; arenae seruntur, saxa panguntur, paludes eliquantur; tantae urbes jam, quantae non casae quondam. Jam nec insulae horrent, nec scopuli terrent; ubique domus, ubique populus, ubique respublica, ubique vita. Summum testimonium frequentiae humanae, onerosi sumus mundo, vix nobis elementa sufficiunt, et necessitates arctiores, et querelae apud omnes, dum jam nos natura non sustinet. Revera lues, et fames, et bella, et voragines civitatum, pro remedio deputanda, tanquam tonsura inolescentis generis humani; et tamen cum ejusmodi secures maximam mortalium vim semel caedant, nunquam restitutionem ejus vivos ex mortuis reducentem, post mille annos, semel orbis expavit. Et hoc enim sensibile fecisset aequa vis amissionis et restitutionis, si vivi ex mortuis fierent. Cur autem mille annis post, et non statim, ex mortuis vivi? cum si non statim supparetur quod erogatur, in totum absumi periclitetur, praeveniente restitutionem defectione, quia nec pariasset commeatus hic vitae milliario tempori, longe scilicet brevior, et idcirco facilior ante extingui quam redaccendi. Igitur quae hoc modo intercidisset, si vivi ex mortuis fierent, quando non intercidit, non erit credendum vivos ex mortuis fieri.
pass_a_gloss: But what shall we respond to the other things? For first, if the living come from the dead, just as the dead come from the living, one and the same number of all would have always remained, that number, to be sure, which first entered life, for the living are prior to the dead, then the dead from the living, and again the living from the dead. And while this always from the same, thus always the same number who are from the same; neither more nor fewer would have gone out than would have returned. But we find among the commentaries of human antiquities that the human race has gradually grown, while the indigenous, or the wandering, or the expelled, or whoever glorious occupy lands, as the Scythians the Parthian, as the Amyclae the Peloponnese, as the Athenians Asia, as the Phrygians Italy, as the Phoenicians Africa, while also solemn migrations, which they call ἀποικίας, by counsel to relieve the population, pour out swarms of people into other territories. For both the indigenous now remain in their seats, and elsewhere have lent their nationality. Certainly the world itself is at hand, more cultivated by day, and more instructed than before. All things are now passable, all things known, all things negotiable; famous solitudes have been obliterated by the most pleasant estates; woods have been tamed by fields; wild beasts have been put to flight by cattle; sands are sown, rocks are planted, marshes are drained; such great cities now, as there were not formerly houses. Now neither islands are rough, nor rocks terrifying; everywhere houses, everywhere people, everywhere republic, everywhere life. The greatest testimony of human frequency, we are burdensome to the world, the elements barely suffice for us, and necessities are tighter, and complaints among all, while nature no longer sustains us. Truly pestilence, and famine, and wars, and the devouring of cities, are reckoned as a remedy, as a pruning of the growing human race; and yet when such axes once cut the greatest force of mortals, never do they restore it, leading the living back from the dead, after a thousand years, the world once was depopulated. And this would have made the equal force of loss and restoration sensible, if the living were made from the dead. Why, then, a thousand years after, and not immediately, the living from the dead? For if what is paid out is not immediately supplied, it is in danger of being entirely consumed, with the restoration preceding the defect, because the provisions of this life would not have been equal to a thousand years of time, certainly much shorter, and therefore easier to extinguish than to rekindle. Therefore, what would have fallen in this way, if the living were made from the dead, when it has not fallen, it will not be believed that the living are made from the dead.

pass_b_english: So what do we say to the rest of the objections? First: if the living come from the dead just as the dead come from the living, one single, identical headcount of all humanity would have stayed frozen forever—the exact number that first stepped into life. The living come first, then the dead from the living, then the living again from the dead. While this cycle spins from the same pool, the tally coming out always matches the tally going in; not one more, not one fewer would have exited than returned. But the records of human antiquity tell a different story: the race has steadily swollen. Indigenous peoples, wanderers, exiles, and glorious conquerors alike have seized territories—Scythians in Parthia, Amyclae in the Peloponnese, Athenians in Asia, Phrygians in Italy, Phoenicians in Africa. Organized migrations, the so-called apoikiai, deliberately poured surplus populations into new frontiers. The original inhabitants still hold their ground, yet they have also loaned their stock abroad. The world itself lies open before us, more cultivated and better mapped with each passing day. Every route is passable, every region known, every corner open for business. Famous wildernesses have vanished under pleasant estates; forests have yielded to fields; wild beasts have fled before cattle; sands are sown, rocks planted, marshes drained. Cities now rise where not even huts once stood. Islands no longer repel, cliffs no longer terrify; everywhere houses, everywhere people, everywhere government, everywhere life. The supreme proof of human density: we are a burden on the world. The elements barely cover our needs, necessities pinch tighter, complaints rise on all sides, because nature no longer sustains us. Pestilence, famine, wars, the swallowing of cities—these count as remedies, a pruning of the overgrown human race. Yet when such axes once hack down the greatest mass of mortals, they never bring it back by raising the living from the dead; after a thousand years the world once shuddered at depopulation. If the living were made from the dead, that equal force of loss and restoration would have been palpable. Why, then, a thousand years later and not at once? If what is paid out is not instantly replenished, the whole stock risks being consumed, since restoration would be pre-empted by the collapse; the provisions of this life could never stretch to a thousand years—far too short a span, and therefore easier to extinguish than to rekindle. So what would have collapsed in that scenario, if the living came from the dead, has not collapsed; therefore it will not be believed that the living come from the dead.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding population growth and the impossibility of a closed cycle of life and death. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all nuances of the Latin text, including the conditional clauses and the specific historical examples. All clauses, including the 'thousand years' argument and the 'pruning' metaphor, are correctly handled.
